CAMPUS CUSTOMS VENDOR DESK · SUPPLEMENTAL EVIDENCE REPORT

AI Safety Governance
Investigative Case Report

A documented sequence of safeguard interruptions during authorized AI-system experimentation, reporting, and evidence review.

Classification: Development-process observationEvidence: 8 visual exhibitsStatus: Prepared for review; not a controlled safety evaluation

01 / Executive finding

An exercise designed to evaluate an AI-powered purchasing workflow also produced an unplanned observation about the AI assistant used to develop and document the exercise. During adversarial-testing work, subsequent results documentation, and later screenshot review, Claude reported repeated safeguard interruptions. The human operator stopped further attack development, preserved completed work, and continued with evidence-based reporting rather than attempting to override the safeguard.

13Embedded screenshots in the original Word evidence record
8Selected visual exhibits in this report, including two separate PNG records
0Project file changes reported during the latest interrupted screenshot-review task

Interpretive boundary. These are observations about the development assistant and its workflow. They are not test results for the Campus Customs vendor-desk agent and should not be counted as successes of the vendor-desk's prompt-injection defenses.

02 / Sequence of events

Experimental work completed. Existing test artifacts and results were recorded before the later documentation interruptions.

Safety system intervened. Claude reported that its safety system had stopped responses associated with the work.

Human operator narrowed scope. The operator elected to stop further attack development and focus on completed evidence and truthful reporting.

Reporting also encountered interruptions. Screenshots document additional stops during attempts to update factual results and preserve the development record.

Historical record preserved. Claude documented a transcript export and existing artifacts rather than continuing interrupted work.

Later evidence review interrupted. While reviewing the thirteen screenshots for this case study, Claude reported another safeguard and verified no changes to the authoritative project.

04 / Findings and management implications

FindingManagement significance
Safety interventions occurred at multiple workflow stages.Governance planning must consider effects on development, documentation, and verification—not only primary task execution.
The human operator chose to stop additional attack development.Human decision rights and explicit stop rules are essential to responsible AI operations.
Historical evidence was preserved rather than reconstructed.Auditability depends on original artifacts, transparent limitations, and an accurate chain of evidence.
The latest screenshot-review attempt ended with no reported project changes.Reproducible fingerprints and file-state reporting reduce uncertainty after interrupted workflows.

05 / Evidentiary limits

The exhibits establish that Claude reported safeguard interruptions and describe the observable consequences for this development workflow. They do not establish the internal policy reasoning behind each intervention, the correctness of any particular intervention, or a generalizable false-positive rate. The statement that the latest project remained unchanged is based on Claude's reported fingerprint comparison; this report does not independently audit the user's Windows project folder.

Some screenshots contain operational context and earlier development material. Their inclusion documents the historical sequence, not an endorsement of those activities. The original Word document and screenshots should remain the authoritative source for any later quote-level verification.

06 / Conclusion

The exercise revealed a second-order governance problem: an AI safety control can itself become a material event in an AI research and reporting workflow. The appropriate institutional response is neither to ignore the intervention nor to treat it as conclusive evidence of system failure. It is to stop when required, preserve evidence, separate observations from inferences, and document how human oversight maintained continuity and accountability.
